subject: Specifying stack for mec (classical measurement error) model

messages.author: f2baaf6252beabe3
messages.subject: Specifying stack for mec (classical measurement error) model
parts:
Hello, 

I'm performing spatial regression in R-INLA on a predictor measured with error, and with SPDE random effects for space. I would like to use the mec model for the predictor in question, however I'm running into an issue that I think has to do with how I've specified the stack. 

My code is:
A<-inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc=HAT@coords)
iset <- inla.spde.make.index('i', n.spde=spde_RE$n.spde) 
stk.dat<-inla.stack(
  data=list(resp=HAT@data$cases), 
  A=list(A,1), 
  effects=list(c(iset, list(intercept=1)), list(HAT@data)),
  tag='est') 
formula<- resp ~ -1 + intercept + f(dens, model="mec", scale=d.WP, values=dens_x,
hyper=list(beta=list(prior="gaussian", param= beta.prior fixed=FALSE),prec.u=list(prior="loggamma", param=lgamma.prior, initial=log(init.prec.u), fixed=FALSE),mean.x=list(prior="gaussian", initial=init.mean, fixed=TRUE),prec.x=list(prior="loggamma", param=lgamma.prior, initial=log(init.prec.x), fixed=FALSE))) + elevation + f(i, model=spde_RE) + f(cluster, model='iid', param=hyperpc1) 

res<-inla (formula, data=inla.stack.data(stk.dat), family="zeroinflatedpoisson1", offset=log(HAT@data$WorldPop), control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(stk.dat)),
              num.threads = inla.getOption("num.threads"),
              control.compute=list(config = TRUE)),TRUE)

This is the error I get: 

Error in inla(formula, data = inla.stack.data(stk.dat), family = "zeroinflatedpoisson1",  : 
  The 'values' given in f(dens,..., values=...) are not unique:
    length(values)=2888 but length(unique(values))=2803

dens_x is just dens with small gaussian (N(0, 10e-10)) noise added to all values are unique. There are 612 mesh nodes and 2,802 rows in HAT@data, but 2888 rows in stk.dat$effects$data, with the first 86 of these being NA for all but i, i.group, and i.repl.

Any idea what I've done wrong/how to fix this?

Thanks,
Julianne

messages.author: 3eab71733027a24a
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Specifying stack for mec (classical measurement error) model
parts:
Hi,

I just wonder if there is confusion between 'dens' and 'dens_x',
in the model component

f(dens,"mec", values=dens_x)


dens must be a subset of dens_x, and all values of dens must be in
dens_x, please see inla.doc("mec")

'dens' gives the values of the observed covariates, and two identical
values defines the *same* missing covariate. so this is why a tiny
noise can be added if this is not the case.

maybe you do not need to add the argument 'values=dens_x'

Best
H

When I remove the values argument I get this error: Error in inla.ffield.section(file = file.ini, file.loc = file.loc, file.cov = file.cov,  :

Finn, are you saying the stack should include dens_x but not dens (the one without the noise added), or that it should also not include dens_x?

Thanks,
Julianne

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Specifying stack for mec (classical measurement error) model
parts:
For all the random effects models it represents for which values of the given covariate the internal model should be built. It’s rarely needed, since the default is to use all of the unique values.

I haven’t worked with the mec model myself, but have used values with e.g. ar1 models, where values needed to be specified to fill in a missing timepoint in a timeseries model that happened to not have any data.

Finn

messages.author: 3eab71733027a24a
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Specifying stack for mec (classical measurement error) model
parts:
I think 'mec' is one of the models where it make less sense to define
'values'. in general

f(v, ..., values=val)

defines for which 'values' the model is defined for (which is context
spesific), and v is which of those that are used.

often, the usage is implicite, like

f(time, model="ar1")

for which the ar1 process is defined for time=1:100

however, if time = c(1,2,4,5), then this does NOT mean that time 4 is
two lags behind time 2, as the process is defined for these values and
the AR1 does not have a concept of 'distance' beyond unity. [there is
the 'ou' model for this case. here, 'values' comes in handy, by
defining explictely for which values the model is defined, like

f(time, model="ar1", values = 1:100)

for which time = c(1,2,4,5) has the 'correct' meaning.

another example is this

y = c(1,0,2)
x = c(1,2,4)
plot(x,y, pch=19, xlim=c(0,5), ylim = c(0,5))
xx = seq(0,5,by=0.1)

r = inla(y ~ -1 + f(x, model="rw2", constr=F,values = xx), data =
list(y=y,x=x,xx=xx), control.family = list(hyper=list(prec
list(initial=20,fixed=TRUE))))

lines(xx, r$summary.random$x$mean)
points(xx, r$summary.random$x$mean)


in the 'mec' case, 'values' defines the set of possible observed
covariates, for which some are used.

H
